content.text: Trees and graphs are the foundational data structures for modeling relationships, hierarchies, and networks in computer science. A tree is a connected acyclic graph where nodes have parent-child relationships, enabling O(log n) operations in balanced variants. A graph generalizes this concept by allowing arbitrary connections between nodes, including cycles, multiple paths, and directed edges. Together, they model everything from file systems and database indexes to social networks and transportation routes.

Mastering trees and graphs requires understanding both the structural properties (balance, connectivity, acyclicity) and the algorithmic techniques (traversal, shortest path, topological ordering) that operate on them. These data structures appear in the majority of system design interviews and are the backbone of production systems including databases, compilers, network routers, and recommendation engines.
This section progresses from fundamental tree operations through graph traversal algorithms to advanced topics like shortest paths and minimum spanning trees.

items: Binary Trees and BSTs — Tree structure, traversals, and binary search tree operations
Balanced Trees and Self-Balancing — AVL, Red-Black trees, and B-Trees for guaranteed performance
Graph Representations and Traversal — Adjacency structures, BFS, DFS, and connected components
Shortest Path Algorithms — Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, and Floyd-Warshall for weighted graphs
Advanced Graph Algorithms — Topological sort, MST, strongly connected components, and network flow
